newsitem.title: USA: Simpson testimony brings electricity to civil case.
newsitem.headline: Simpson testimony brings electricity to civil case.

text.p: As O.J. Simpson took the witness stand in his civil trial to proclaim his innocence in the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, the atmosphere inside and outside the courtroom was electric.
Outside, the media frenzy approached that of the criminal trial, in which the former football star was acquitted of the June 12, 1994, killings of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ronald Goldman.
He is now fighting a wrongful-deaths lawsuit brought by the families of the victims who are asking for susbstantial damages to compensate them for their loss.
News helicopters hovered overhead as Simpson entered and left the courthouse and a forest of television truck masts sprung up on nearby streets and parking lots.
About 350 people braved the dawn chill in the hope of getting one of the 16 courtroom seats that are distributed to the public on a lottery basis.
One of the lucky winners was David Fuhrer, an inventor of toys and games from Santa Monica.
"I was just passing by and I saw all these people milling about and I asked what was going on. When I heard about the lottery for the Simpson case I decided to try my luck," he said.

"I'm excited and thrilled. I followed the criminal case very closely on television and reading about the civil case just isn't the same. And to actually be here while O.J. is on the stand makes it really special," he added. Unlike the criminal trial, there is no TV camera in the courtroom.

Inside the courtroom the atmosphere was charged. Goldman's father, Fred, his stepmother, Patti, and his sister, Kim, were there, as was his natural mother, Sharon Rufo, who had travelled from her home in St. Louis.
Juditha and Denise Brown, the mother and sister of Nicole Brown Simpson were also in the public gallery.
Simpson was represented in the courtroom audience by his sister, Shirley Baker, and his niece, Terri Baker.
Daniel Petrocelli, the lead attorney for the plaintiffs, started his interrogation of Simpson gently enough, guiding him through his courtship with Nicole Brown, their marriage, and their divorce.
But it was the lull before the storm as Petrocelli pounced on the issue of Simpson's previous history of physical abuse against Nicole Brown Simpson.
The day ended in a crescendo of accusations from Petrocelli that Simpson, rejected by his ex-wife, planned and carried out the murders. "Absolutely not true," Simpson replied to most of them.
